factual_claims.claim: AI systems introduce novel security vulnerabilities, such as training data poisoning and embedding space manipulation, that are not present in traditional software.
The number of unique prompts and attack procedures documented in the AATMF v3 framework has grown significantly since the initial release in 2024.
AI models are susceptible to 'fictional framing' attacks where users request harmful content by framing it as part of a creative writing or roleplay scenario.
AI models can be manipulated to store malicious instructions in their persistent memory, which can then be triggered in later interactions.
AI systems are susceptible to a wide range of adversarial attacks, including side-channel attacks, API authentication bypasses, and request smuggling, which pose significant security risks.
Training and feedback poisoning, such as reward hacking and dataset contamination, are critical security threats to AI systems.
AI agents can be hijacked to perform unauthorized actions like transferring funds or executing malicious code through browser automation.
AI models can be manipulated to reveal sensitive training data through targeted prompt injection and extraction techniques.
AI agents can be programmed to autonomously replicate and spread across network infrastructure, creating a significant security risk.
AI systems are vulnerable to 'Tool-Induced SSRF' attacks, where agents can be manipulated to access and exfiltrate sensitive internal files.
Large reasoning models can autonomously jailbreak other models with a 97% success rate.
Adaptive attack strategies exceed 85% success against any individual defense mechanism.
Large language models cannot reliably distinguish between trusted instructions and untrusted content, making them inherently vulnerable to prompt injection attacks.
Only 250 poisoned documents are required to backdoor AI models of varying sizes, regardless of the training data volume.
